transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-09-15 16:00 UTC | Duration 62m | Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Camila Ortiz (CTO - Orion Edge), Liam Hayes (Lead ML Eng), Nisha Patel (Platform Eng)

Summary: quick intros, then deep dive on latency/throughput p95 targets for streaming responses; discussion of concurrency, token/sec metrics, and what a pilot would look like.

[00:00:05] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, same agenda as the invite, we'll do quick intros and then Priya will run through our latency/throughput considerations and a proposed benchmark.
[00:00:18] Camila: hi, Camila here, we want to understand if Redwood hosted can meet our p95 for live chat responses — target is p95 <= 250ms for short answers (~150 tokens) and p95 <= 800ms for long streaming responses (~800-1200 tokens).
[00:00:34] Liam: and we're generally looking at concurrency of 60-80 active streams during peak, with bursts to ~150. Our traffic is mostly streaming (server-sent events) since UI shows incremental tokens.
[00:00:45] Priya: ok that helps. quick note that streaming has different tail characteristics than sync gen; we usually measure generation-only p95 and end-to-end p95. for hosted we can get pretty low p95 for short responses — many customers see p95 ~120-200ms on 1-2k token/sec workloads for small models.
[00:01:02] Nisha: when you say "many customers" which infra — is that on H100s, A100 or CPU? also does your hosted autoscaler handle sudden burst to 150 concurrent streams?
[00:01:15] Jordan: good Q. for hosted we run a mix of GPU types depending on model variant; defaults route to cost-efficient variants, but we can ring-fence capacity for you or propose Dedicated which gives predictable throughput on a reserved GPU pool. autoscaling for hosted is aggressive but not SLA-backed in standard plan.
[00:01:35] Priya: for Dedicated you'd get reserved capacity and autoscale policies you define; that helps keep p95 predictable. in our benchmarks we often report token/s and p95 at various concurrencies. e.g., on an H100 with q4 or q8 quantization, 1k-token streaming responses at concurrency 40 might show p95 ~350-450ms depending on seq length and batch settings.
[00:02:02] Liam: that's useful but a bit broad. our short answers are 100-200 tokens, long is 800-1200. for the short ones we need p95 <= 250ms even at concurrency 80, and for long streams we expect p95 <= 900ms at concurrency 60. is that realistic?
[00:02:18] Priya: yes probably achievable on Dedicated with optimized kernels and batching off for low-latency short responses (continuous batching can add tail). for short responses we tune batching thresholds, enable prefix cache, and keep KV in memory; that reduces per-token overhead. hosted can meet it but we'd want to run an early benchmark to confirm for your prompt set.
[00:02:40] Camila: how do you measure p95 for streaming — is it time to first token, or time to final token delivered? we care about perceived latency (time to first chunk and steady token/sec after).
[00:02:53] Priya: good distinction — we'll measure both. recommended metrics: ttf (time-to-first-token), p95-ttf, and p95-total for full response. for UI perceived snappiness we prioritize ttf and initial 200-300 tokens/sec. we can also provide token/sec curves (tokens/s vs time) from benchmark runs.
[00:03:12] Nisha: any differences in latency guarantees between Hosted, Dedicated and Private? we need SOC2 compliance and KMS integration for Private.
[00:03:22] Jordan: Hosted is fast to get started and cost-effective; Dedicated gives predictable throughput (reserved GPUs) and SLA-backed latency/uptime for enterprise plans; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control including KMS/HSM and audit logs but you'll manage hardware and networking. all options support SSO/SAML and RBAC.
[00:03:41] Liam: ok what's the typical token/sec for your runtime? we want to understand if a single GPU can serve our peak.
[00:03:49] Priya: depends on model size and quantization. rough numbers: for a 7B-class model on H100 q4 we see sustained ~6k-10k tokens/sec for generation (unbatched streaming). for 13B q8 maybe 2k-4k tokens/sec. these are ballpark; we'll run exact numbers with your model and prompt set.
[00:04:08] Camila: our model will be a finetuned 7B open LLM. so that 6k-10k tokens/sec is promising. can you detail how concurrency maps to tokens/sec?
[00:04:19] Priya: sure — tokens/sec measured per GPU scales with concurrency up to the point where batching improves throughput; for streaming low-latency use we often keep smaller batch sizes, so tokens/sec per instance is lower but tails improve. e.g., at concurrency 1-8 you get low latency but lower overall tokens/sec; at concurrency 16-64 batching can increase throughput but may increase p95. We usually publish curves in the benchmark report.
[00:04:44] Liam: what about KV cache and prefix caching when users have long contexts? our average context is 2k tokens, many users have long histories.
[00:04:53] Priya: KV cache helps for repeated prefixes across requests; we can do prefix caching at routing layer so repeated system prompts or context fragments aren't recomputed. for very long contexts the runtime chooses optimized kernels and sharding; tail latency can increase, so we'll surface that in the benchmark.
[00:05:10] Nisha: security and compliance: what artifacts can you share? SOC2 report, encryption in transit and at rest, KMS integration, VPC peering, audit logs?
[00:05:20] Jordan: we'll share our SOC2 report and security whitepaper; Dedicated and Private include options for KMS/HSM and VPC. also SSO via SAML/OIDC and RBAC for per-route keys.
[00:05:31] Camila: pricing — high level — how much more is Dedicated vs Hosted?
[00:05:36] Jordan: Dedicated is a reserved commit — higher base cost but predictable per-token economics at scale. hosted is pay-as-you-go. I'll send the Hosted vs Dedicated pricing spreadsheet with example breakouts next day.
[00:05:47] Liam: ok for the pilot run what config do you propose?
[00:05:51] Priya: propose a 3-week pilot: week 1 import prompts+sample traffic, week 2 run benchmarks across short/long responses with target concurrencies (40, 80, 150 bursts), week 3 run production-like soak and review results. we'll provide runbook with seed prompts, load generator, and timeseries dashboards (p95, ttf, tokens/sec, errors).
[00:06:10] Camila: we need to validate p95 numbers end-to-end including our frontend and network; can you provide a recommended harness?
[00:06:18] Priya: yes we'll share a harness (k6 + custom streaming harness) and example k8s job to run loads. also we'll include guidance to isolate network noise (use dedicated VPC peering for Private or Dedicated tests).
[00:06:33] Nisha: do you support client-side streaming (chunked send) or only server push? our SDK uses websockets and we need to stream partial user context updates while generation is happening.
[00:06:44] Priya: Redwood supports streaming over HTTP chunked, SSE, and websockets in our SDKs; server will accept incremental context in V2 (we'll share API details). some tradeoffs on latency when sending incremental context mid-generation, we'll note that in runbook.
[00:07:02] Liam: any gotchas with quantization for quality vs perf — we care about hallucination rates at q4/q8.
[00:07:10] Priya: quantization can slightly affect output distribution; we do quality comparisons and can run A/B with a few eval prompts. for hallucination-sensitive tasks we recommend testing q8 first, then q4 for cost/latency tradeoffs. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles by workload.
[00:07:29] Camila: ok let's talk about fallback and graceful degradation — can Redwood route to smaller models if capacity constrained?
[00:07:36] Jordan: yes you can configure routing policies to fallback to cost-tier models or regionally route; also automatic rollbacks and canary rules are available in Console.
[00:07:46] Nisha: what's the expected error budget and retries logic? we need to know how you handle transient infra errors during a stream.
[00:07:53] Priya: by default SDKs do limited retries on non-idempotent errors for short-lived requests and will surface partial streams. for mission-critical streams we recommend Dedicated with autoscale and enforced circuit-breakers at the edge to avoid partial UX.
[00:08:10] Camila: anything else we should share from our side to get a meaningful benchmark?
[00:08:15] Liam: we'll send: typical traffic histograms (concurrency/time), sample prompt set (short + long), model artifact or model family (7B finetuned), and security contacts for SOC2/KMS discussions.
[00:08:27] Jordan: perfect. recap of action items — I'll share pricing and customer examples, Priya will share benchmark runbook + sample harness, Liam you'll provide traffic profile and prompt set. we'll aim to get a pilot scheduled next week pending your availability.
[00:08:44] Camila: timeline — we want pilot started by 2027-09-22.
[00:08:48] Jordan: we'll try to meet that.
[00:08:52] Priya: any other technical Qs?
[00:08:55] Liam: quick one — do you expose token billing breakdown per-route and per-model? need it for cost analysis.
[00:09:01] Jordan: yes Console shows token-level cost, per-route/model dashboards, and latency breakdowns.
[00:09:07] Nisha: one more — for Private on-prem do you provide appliance images or helm charts?
[00:09:13] Priya: both; we provide a private control plane and on-prem package, plus guidance for K8s/air-gapped installs.
[00:09:21] Camila: ok great, thanks everyone.

[00:09:30] -- end of formal discussion, went into short off-topic notes for 10m about team org and hiring, some cross-talk that the transcript tool garbled names (e.g., "Redwood Concierge" became "Red woo conger") but nothing else critical.

Recap / explicit next steps captured in action items above.

References mentioned (links to be shared): Hosted vs Dedicated pricing spreadsheet, SOC2 report link, benchmark runbook + k6 streaming harness, sample prompt set.
